text: Security and entitlements One policy language, one decision point, many enforcement points. Policy is written once in OPA and projected into every engine, because hand-granting access in five places is how the fifth goes wrong. Question Where it is answered How sensitive is this? Classification and tags per column in the data contract Where is personal information? Presidio at ingestion, before Silver Who are you, and may you do this? Single identity provider with MFA; OPA evaluates role and attribute together Who holds which grant, why, until when? The entitlement register, reviewed quarterly Which rows may you see? Row-level security in Postgres; per-tenant views in the lakehouse Can identifiers be reversed? Keyed HMAC-SHA3, never plain hashes; the re-identification crosswalk stays in South Africa Can the network be trusted? Cilium policy between workloads; an egress allowlist for external services Can data be retired? Per-client keys: destroying the key retires the data, even inside history The boundary filters what enters, never what leaves: the context before the model, the IR before the solver, the join before the query. text: Quantum readiness Quantum computing threatens today's signatures, not the hash chain. The ledger is built to the NIST post-quantum standards now, and keeps a seam open for quantum solvers later. HashingSHA3-256 (FIPS 202) chains the ledger; BLAKE3 serves only as a fast content digest. SignaturesML-DSA (FIPS 204) signs each entry; SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), resting only on hashes, signs periodic checkpoints. Key exchangeML-KEM (FIPS 203) in hybrid TLS protects data in transit against harvest-now, decrypt-later. Crypto-agilityEvery entry records its hash and signature algorithm, so successors can be adopted without rewriting history. Solver seamThe IR names its solver. Optimisation problems can be exported for quantum trials, on anonymised formulations only.

section: The eight planes of the Spine
text: The eight planes of the Spine The Spine is a portable core that carries an organisation from raw evidence, through identity and meaning, through adaptation to the situation at hand, to a solved and explained decision, bounded in execution and returned to strategy as correction. Plane The question it answers Rate of change L0 Strategy Intent What are we trying to achieve, and what will we not do? Quarterly to annual L1 Evidence What arrived, and what did it become? Continuous append L2 Identity Who and what is this about? Continuous, reversible L3 Meaning What do these things mean, and how are they computed? Slow, by deliberation only L4 Adaptation What applies here, now, to this case, and has the world moved? Fast: the only fast plane L5 Judgement What is the best feasible decision, and what does it cost? Per decision, generated L6 Foresight What might happen, and what if we chose otherwise? Per query, over the same IR L7 Execution & Feedback What was done, within what bounds, and what actually happened? Continuous Evidence rises and gains identity, then meaning. Intent descends and gains constraint. They meet at Adaptation, which fits both to the present case and hands a situated program to Judgement. Three planes are slow, one is fast, and the fast one is isolated, so change has somewhere legitimate to live. The storage engines beneath are stubs; the core between them is what Ingqiqo owns.

text: Two legs, one identity The lakehouse holds what happened. The lakebase holds what is being done. Master data is the bridge, so both legs agree on who and what every record is about. The lakehouse leg DuckLake as catalog and table format, with snapshots and time travel. Organised as a data mesh: each domain, modelled with domain-driven design, owns its slice from Bronze to Gold. A logical data fabric virtualises access across domains without copying data. The master data bridge Multi-domain mastering of party, employment, location, asset, contract and product. Match rules are generated from the ontology, not hand-coded: Zingg resolves entities and feeds AtroCore. Identity is held as a registry; attributes are read from the source of record. The lakebase leg Postgres as the operational store for applications, the decision ledger and workflow state. Polars works the frames on the application side, and apps follow the open Databricks Apps pattern. Row-level security and point-in-time restore are part of the port, not optional extras. One rule keeps the legs honest: a live, virtualised read may serve an application, but it may never enter a decision. Anything a decision rests on is first snapshotted and hashed.

text: The medallion Three tiers, each with one job. History is never overwritten, and every interpretation can be argued with and re-derived. BronzeRaw and immutable. SilverData Vault 2.0: hubs for business keys, links for relationships, satellites for history. Insert-only, source-aligned, so it can always answer what was known at the time. text: The semantic layer DuckDB and Polars share one semantic layer, so a metric means the same thing in SQL and in code. On it, nineteen models are given life, grouped by the question each family answers. Meaning Terminology · Taxonomy · Ontological · Semantic · Meaning · Context Structure Data · Process · Application · Business Rule Mind Cognitive · Memory · Evaluation Decision Decision · Outcome · Coherence Accountability Motive · Ownership · Institutional Architecture Meaning changes slowly and by deliberation. text: Judgement Every decision is compiled into one typed, content-addressed program: the Decision IR. Strategy, ontology terms, mastered identities, business rules and evidence all compile into it, and nothing bypasses it. Rules first. GoRules decides eligibility, routing and which constraints apply to this case at all, in milliseconds and editable by a domain expert. Then the Sovereign Logic Engine. Weighted MaxSMT on Z3, over DPLL(T) and CDCL search. Hard constraints must hold; soft constraints carry the weights the organisation says it values. The cost of the answer is the product. When soft constraints cannot all be met, the engine returns the minimum-weight set it relaxed. No plan is issued without the commitment it broke to get there. Self-subtraction. Constraints that never bind are demoted, then removed; objectives that never bind are retired. Every removal is recorded and reversible.

text: Estimators and AI influence Tabular in-context-learning models (TabDPT-Turbo and TabICLv2) and Laya, an open-source model, make the platform useful from week one on a client's modest data. They also change what the data, the AI and the decisions owe each other. On the data In context learning, the client's rows are the prompt. Membership is not inferred; it is read. Entitlement therefore filters the context before it is assembled, never the answer after. Context rows, their order and the decoding policy are pinned in the evidence manifest so results replay. On AI influence The neural proposes; the symbolic disposes. No model asserts a constraint, sets a weight or emits a decision. Laya is open source, so it runs inside the client’s own boundary, where its weights can be inspected and its runs pinned, and nothing leaves the jurisdiction. Behavioural parameters are declared, versioned and switchable, never hidden in the interface. On decisions These models are correlational. They estimate what tends to happen, not what happens if we intervene. Every IR variable carries an endogenous flag, and binding a correlational estimate to a decision variable is a compile-time error. Outputs are distributions, and the uncertainty survives into the solver. For sweeps that would fire thousands of predictions, the ICL model teaches a cheap deterministic surrogate that runs the inner loop, which also restores determinism where the solver needs it. Model versions named here are checked against current published benchmarks before any design is frozen.

text: Accountability, traced back A good outcome is not a good decision. Outcomes are assessed against what drove the decision, who owned it, and the institution it was made inside. Outcome ModelWhat actually happened, scored separately from the quality of the process, which is fixed at decision time and never revised after the fact. Motive ModelWhat each actor was trying to achieve, and which drivers the decision design covered. Institutional Architecture ModelThe Moloto Framework’s seven structural elements: authority, information, discretion, incentives, advancement, procedure and consequence. It separates the formal architecture from the one that actually operates. Used in this methodology with the kind consent of Thabang Sir Moloto, to whom I am grateful. Ownership ModelWho held the decision, the authority and the consequence, at each step. The nine-step IDDCThe Ingqiqo Disciplined Decision Cycle (discover, connect, review, facilitate, compare, consolidate, publish, execute, learn) reads the Ownership Model against the Motive Model at every step. Where they clash, it shows whether culpability was manufactured by design, and traces the chain back to the original actor or mover. Findings climb a fixed ladder (flag, anomaly, investigation, finding, attribution, culpability) and describe machinery, not intent. Three assurance axes, decision integrity, decision validity and attribution integrity, are reported side by side and never collapsed into one score.

text: The Decision Warranty The warranty promises process fidelity, not good outcomes: that a decision was made as specified, on the evidence recorded, by the authority named. It is a contractual warranty on the service, not insurance. What it warrants The Decision IR, its evidence hash and its relaxation set, checked against the four assurance disciplines: integrity, validity, conscience and optimisation. A companion Agency Warranty covers the actors who carry the decision out. How it is evidenced Every warranted decision is written to a hash-chained ledger and signed. The Intrinsic Coverage Instrument records whether the design covered what motivates the people it affects, and flags an exception where it did not. What stands behind it Liability caps and a written claims procedure, an ISO 27001-aligned security programme, professional indemnity and cyber cover, and a legal opinion on the structure. Where risk transfer is wanted, a licensed insurer underwrites and the ledger supplies the evidence.

text: Instruments · Governance and maturity Decision governance and maturity Most organisations cannot say who is entitled to decide what, on what evidence, accountable to whom. text: The method The Ingqiqo Disciplined Decision Cycle Every instrument we deliver is a scripted run of one cycle, IDDC, which turns evidence and meaning into decisions that can be checked, contested and repeated. No stage may be skipped because a client is in a hurry. I Discover Find the decision, the people who hold it, and the evidence that exists. II Connect Tie the evidence to shared meaning: terms, entities and relationships. III Review Test the evidence and the assumptions against a clear standard. IV Facilitate Bring the decision-holders together on the same picture. V Compare Lay out the alternatives, and what each one gives up. VI Consolidate Settle on one decision, recorded with its evidence and authority. VII Publish Release it as a governed record that others can rely on and contest. VIII Execute Carry it out within declared bounds, watching for deviation. IX Learn Score the outcome separately from the process, and feed the difference back. Three commitments hold at every size: method, not headcount; instruments, not one-off reports; working shown, not hidden.

text: The method in practice Six disciplines in every run Name the decision, and its owner. Before anything is measured. A diagnostic with no decision attached is a report, and reports do not change anything. Define the unit. What exactly is being counted: one offer, one approval, one hour, one claim. A total built without this step is a number nobody can defend, and it will still print. Measure what is there. The client's own tables and their own people, sampled anonymously. We do not substitute a sector average for a measurement we could have taken. Calculate, and mark every figure. One results file. Each figure carries how it came to be (observed, declared, published or estimated) and a range where estimated. Render for each reader. One results file, several views: finance, operations, technology, employee relations, organised labour, staff, the executive. Different weightings, never different numbers. Set the review date. Every significant recommendation carries the date it will be judged against what actually happened. This is the step that makes the second run worth buying. Why the discipline is written down A method held in one person's head cannot be audited, delegated or improved. IDDC is documented end to end and version-stamped on every output, which is what allows an accredited associate to run an instrument, a client to check it, and a successor supplier to pick it up. The full formal statement (its units, its memory horizons, its treatment of estimates) is set out in The Coherence Architecture, available under NDA where a technical evaluation requires it.

text: B.3 Theory of welfare, for signature Completed at kick-off and countersigned. We redesign the context in which decisions are made: defaults, sequencing, evidence, thresholds, templates. That is an intervention in how people choose, so whose interest it serves is stated rather than assumed. Primary interest [stated, e.g. long-term value of the organisation] Freedom Every default has a clear, low-cost way to choose otherwise. Friction that serves the institution against the chooser is out of scope. Secondary interests [stated, e.g. employees affected by the process; customers or citizens affected by its outcomes] Publicity We will not implement anything we would be unwilling to disclose to those it affects. Each intervention is documented in plain language. Where they conflict We will say so and escalate the trade-off to [named executive] for decision. We will not settle it silently through design. Endorsement We steer only toward choices the affected decision-makers would endorse on reflection, and we check that with them rather than assume it. Capability Each redesign builds your people’s own decision capability, so sustaining it does not depend on us. Measurement Each intervention has a baseline, a stated expected effect and a review date. We report results, including null and negative ones. Contestability Anyone affected may challenge an intervention through [named channel]. Challenges are logged and answered. Reversibility Every intervention has a named owner and can be withdrawn if the evidence or the affected stakeholders do not support it. Register Every intervention is entered in a register held by you: purpose, whose interest it serves, the opt-out path, expected and measured effect, owner, review date, status. An intervention whose assumptions have expired is withdrawn rather than left running. Signed for Ingqiqo Executables Signed for the client Date On the size of the claim. Interventions of this kind, measured honestly in real organisations, move outcomes by low single-digit percentage points, far below what published studies report. text: C.1 Questions your executive will ask Our answers, in advance, so your sponsor can answer them without waiting for us to be in the room. “We already have dashboards, BI and AI. What is different?” Dashboards present information. What we produce is a record of the transition from evidence to authorised action: intent, assumptions, evidence and its pedigree, alternatives, constraints, who decided, and what actually followed. The differentiator is not a better chart; it is that the decision itself becomes inspectable afterwards. “Isn’t this just change management?” It overlaps and goes lower. Change management asks how people adopt a change. We ask how this organisation repeatedly produces choices and commitments under uncertainty, and then alter the templates, thresholds and sequencing that produce them. “Our decisions are too unique to standardise.” We do not standardise the judgement. We standardise the scaffolding around it: what evidence is required, how options are structured, who decides, what gets recorded, and how the outcome is checked. Discretion is preserved inside explicit constraints; that is the whole design. “What is the return, in a number I can defend?” We cost the friction in the flow we are given (delay, rework, error rate multiplied by stakes) against a baseline agreed before we start, and report what moved at ninety days. We will not quote you a percentage from someone else’s study. On a flow of any size, a small measured improvement is a large number; an unmeasured large one is a dispute waiting to happen. “Who loses discretion if this works?” The right question, and we will raise it if you do not. Making decision rights explicit exposes who actually decides, on what evidence. Some resistance to this work is not about priorities; it is about that exposure. We will name where we expect it, and we will not pretend the engagement is politically weightless.

text: B.1 What we warrant, and what we do not The Decision Warranty promises process fidelity, not outcomes: that a decision was made as specified, on the evidence recorded, by the authority named. It is a warranty on our service. It is not insurance. The right-hand column is the one that matters; a commitment without stated exclusions is a sales line that gets disclaimed in an annexure nobody read. We stand behind The arithmetic. Every figure re-derivable from the inputs supplied at the stamped versions. Our error is ours to correct at our cost. That the method was followed. Each output meets the published standard item by item, checkable by anyone. That the pedigree is honest. Nothing estimated is shown as observed. Estimates carry ranges. Thin sources are labelled thin. That it reproduces. Same inputs, same versions, same answer. If not, that is a defect and we treat it as one. That the record is complete. Each machine contribution is logged as a proposal, with who accepted or rejected it. That the data is handled as agreed. A finding does not guarantee a saving. What happens next is a decision we name but do not take. Inputs we did not measure. A figure you supply is marked declared. We warrant our use of it, not its accuracy. Individual behaviour. An estimate is a probability over a population. No output of ours is evidence about an identified person. Legal, tax, audit or actuarial conclusions. We are not registered to give them. Where one is needed we name who should. Compliance itself. Our governance work supports obligations under King IV and the employment statutes. It does not discharge them. Insurance. The warranty is on our process. It does not transfer your risk to us. text: 2.4 How committed work is tracked Work that has been committed moves through six named states. Each is written into the record, so that what happened to an item can be read rather than remembered. Committed Agreed at kick-off and entered in the tracker, with its owner and target week. In progress Work has started, and sits with the owner the tracker names. Deviated What is happening differs from what was committed. Recorded when it is noticed, not reconstructed later. Contained The deviation has been limited, and its effect on other items is stated. Escalated The deviation is beyond what its owner can contain, and has been taken to a person with authority to decide. Verified The work has been checked against the acceptance test agreed at kick-off. The principle Fidelity is assessed before the outcome is finalised Whether the work was carried out as committed is read from the record first, and written down. Only then is the outcome read. A good outcome is not a good decision, and the record keeps the two apart. These states are kept alongside the Status column, not in place of it. They add no threshold to the measures in Part III.
title: The Progress Record

text: PART III The instrument Six standard delivery measures, one arithmetic correction, a worked example — and an honest account of what the same six measures look like when we are the party at fault.
title: The Progress Record

text: 3.1 Six measures of flow Measure What it is What it exposes Flow efficiency Active work time as a share of total elapsed time; the remainder is wait How much of the window was ever workable, and who imposed each wait Flow velocity Completed items per unit time Throughput — but only honestly when divided by available capacity rather than the calendar Flow predictability Planned against actual completions over time, read per workstream Exactly where plan and reality diverge — usually at an ownership boundary, not a date Flow time Start to completion per item; for open items, aging beyond target Whether overruns are general or confined to one class of owner Flow distribution How the remaining open work is allocated across owners Whether the critical path still runs through the supplier at all Flow load Open work carried per individual role, on both sides Single-point concentration — the structural bottleneck that no additional effort from anyone can relieve Nothing proprietary. These are the metrics any competent delivery organisation uses on its own work, applied to ours — which is the point. An assessment framework invented by the supplier being assessed is worth less than one anybody can look up. On flow load and people When this measure finds that seven of eight open items sit with one person on your side, that is a finding about your operating design and not about them. No role in any delivery system absorbs that load without becoming the constraint. We report it as a structure, and the remedy is to fan the ownership out — never to name an individual as the cause. What these measures cannot tell you Whether the work was any good. Flow metrics count completions, not quality — an item marked done can still be wrong. Quality is judged against the acceptance test agreed at kick-off, and a supplier who scores well here and badly there has gamed a tracker.
title: The Progress Record

text: 3.2 Tools calculate; named people judge The machines calculate. People do the thinking. Every reading in this booklet is calculated and recorded by a tool, and judged by a named person on each side. Handed to the tools Calculating — the six measures, from the tracker and the register alone. Retrieving — each figure, with its source line in the tracker. Proposing — a reading of each measure, marked as a proposal. Recording — what was proposed, what was accepted, and by whom. Stays with people Framing — what the decision is, and whose. Judgement — what counts, and what trade-off is acceptable. Deciding — a named person with authority signs. Accountability — who answers, and when it is reviewed. Named on both sides Judging the readings for the client: [named] Judging the readings for Ingqiqo: [named] The record can find against either party No tool decides who failed. A reading is a proposal that a named person accepts or rejects, and each acceptance is recorded. The record can find against us, as page 17 sets out. It can find against you too, and reports it as a structure, never as a person. People decide; every machine contribution is a recorded proposal. The Progress workbook keeps the same record digitally.

text: 3.3 The denominator problem One arithmetic choice decides most progress disputes: what you divide completed work by. Both readings below use the same numerator and the same tracker. Reading one · the calendar Planned 24 activities over 6 weeks Planned rate 4.0 / week Completed 16 Elapsed 6 weeks 2.7 / week 67% of the planned rate. Reads unambiguously as under-delivery, and every level of an organisation will read it that way. Reading two · available capacity Planned 30 working days Less logged impairments 15 days Available 3 weeks Completed 16 5.3 / week 133% of the planned rate through half the planned capacity. Same work, same record, opposite conclusion. Why reading two is not special pleading Because the impairments were logged in the week they occurred, by both parties, with the side recorded before anyone had a position — and because the same subtraction is applied to our own impairments, which reduce the denominator in your favour. Reading two is only honest if the register was kept honestly. That is the whole reason page 10 comes before this page, and why an unlogged impairment is forfeited rather than argued. Where reading two is not available to us On consultant-owned items with no logged impairment against them. There the calendar is the correct denominator and we will not offer another. If sixteen of twenty-four were ours to finish unimpeded and we finished eleven, the honest figure is eleven and the finding is against us.
title: The Progress Record

text: 3.4 A worked assessment Anonymised from a real engagement in which an adverse progress assessment had been formed. Twenty-four activities, seven workstreams, a six-week window. Read the right-hand column before drawing a conclusion from the middle one. Workstream Planned Done Owner of the remainder Scope and start gate 3 3 — Access and schema 4 4 — Reverse-engineering 3 3 — Data product build 4 4 — Governance and security 3 1 1 client · 1 joint, client-gated Testing and acceptance 4 1 1 client SMEs · 2 client sign-off Close-out and next scope 3 0 2 client · 1 joint, client-gated Total 24 16 8 open · 0 solely consultant-owned Consultant-owned 14 / 14 complete, all within target week Client-gated 2 / 10 complete — where all variance sits Aging of open items 31–59 days past target, none of it ours Flow load 7 / 8 open items on one client role What the divergence point tells you Completions tracked plan almost exactly through week four, then flattened — at precisely the point in the schedule where ownership transferred to client-side roles. The variance the executives saw was real. It simply lived on the other side of the ownership boundary, and the assessment was formed during a further thirty-one days in which nothing moved and nothing awaited us.

text: PART IV The finding How a finding is written so it can be contested, what remedy each class of finding actually warrants, and the assumptions every figure rests on.
title: The Progress Record

text: 4.1 How findings are written Specimen findings, from the worked assessment F1 Capacity. Roughly half the planned window was consumed by wait states, two-thirds of them client-controlled. The efficiency loss was imposed rather than incurred. F2 Velocity. Throughput per available week was 5.3 activities — 133% of the planned rate. The slow-progress reading is an artefact of using the calendar rather than available capacity as the denominator. F3 Predictability. All consultant-owned activities completed to plan. The entire plan-against-actual variance sits in client-gated workstreams, at 20% complete. F4 Flow time. No consultant-owned item overran. All aging, between 31 and 59 days, is on client-owned or client-gated items. F5 Distribution. No open item is solely consultant-owned. The critical path no longer passes through the supplier. F6 Load. Open-work ownership is concentrated on a single client-side role, at seven of eight items — a structural bottleneck that no additional supplier effort can relieve. F7 Timing. The adverse assessment was formed during a 31-day post-window period in which every open item awaited client action. One numbered finding per measure, plus a final one on the timing of the assessment itself. Each states the measure, the figure, the source line in the tracker, and the conclusion — in that order, so the conclusion can be rejected while the figure stands. Why figure and conclusion are separated So you can accept F2’s arithmetic and still reject its inference. A finding that fuses the two forces you to argue with a number in order to disagree with an opinion, which is how reviews turn adversarial. Your dissent goes in the document Where you disagree with a finding, your words are recorded beside it, unedited, over your attribution. We do not issue an assessment that contains only our own reading of a jointly held record.
title: The Progress Record

section: You are entitled to conclude that we failed
text: Read this first You are entitled to conclude that we failed At some point in an engagement a client looks at what they are paying for and asks whether it was worth it. Sometimes the honest answer is no. That judgement belongs to you, and nothing in this booklet is an attempt to take it away. What this booklet does is make the judgement measurable rather than impressionistic — and it hands you the instrument in advance, at kick-off, before either of us knows which way it will point. That timing is the entire design. An assessment method produced after a dispute has begun is an argument. The same method agreed beforehand is evidence. We have been on the receiving end of an adverse progress assessment. It was formed in good faith, from a reasonable reading of a calendar, and it was wrong — not because the client was careless but because the tracker’s own ownership column had never been read alongside its status column. That experience produced this instrument. It is published because a supplier who only reaches for telemetry once it is accused has produced a defence, not a discipline. The commitment The instrument is symmetrical Every measure here can produce a finding against us, and page 17 states exactly what such a finding looks like and what we owe you when it appears. A fairness assessment that can only exonerate the party who wrote it is not an assessment. The standing Not a legal instrument This creates no obligation and overrides nothing. Where it and a signed agreement differ, the agreement governs. It is a shared method for reading a record you already hold — and your right to terminate on whatever grounds your contract permits is untouched by it. The ambition is narrow and worth stating plainly: that when you decide we failed, you are right — and that when you decide we did not, you can show someone why.

text: 4.2 Proportionate remedy The measures diagnose; they do not decide. But a diagnosis does narrow the sensible responses, and matching them is what separates a review from a reflex. Where the finding lands Proportionate Ineffective, however satisfying Consultant under-delivery on owned items Completion at our cost, revised dates set by you, or termination — your call, and all three are legitimate Adding scope to recover goodwill Client-side dependency queue A dependency recovery plan: fan ownership out, name dates, escalate the gates Terminating the supplier — the queue survives the change and so does the delay Single-point load, either side Redistribute ownership; add a named deputy for the gating role Pressing the overloaded person harder Wait states on both sides Re-baseline the window against available capacity and re-plan jointly Holding the original date and calling the shortfall a performance issue Scope was wrong from the start Stop, re-scope, and treat the spend as the cost of finding out Pushing on because the budget is committed On termination It is always available to you and we will not contest it. What we ask is narrower: that if it is exercised on progress grounds, the tracker’s ownership column has been read alongside its status column first. A termination that penalises the only party whose work is complete does not recover the programme — it restarts the same queue with a new supplier and a month of onboarding added to it. We would rather be dismissed on an accurate finding than retained on an inaccurate one. The second outcome costs us the next engagement anyway, and costs you the month it takes to discover the queue was never ours.

text: 1.2 Why impression gets it wrong Not because executives are careless. Because the three things most visible from a distance are the three least diagnostic, and they all point the same way. Visible The calendar Six weeks were agreed; six weeks have passed; two-thirds of the list is done. That reads as under-delivery at every level of an organisation. It says nothing about how many of those thirty days were actually workable — and wait states do not appear on a calendar, which is precisely why they go unpriced. Visible The open-item count Eight things are not finished. The count is accurate and the inference from it is not: a status column read without the owner column beside it cannot distinguish work nobody did from work nobody could do. Those are opposite findings with opposite remedies. Visible The silence Nothing has moved for a month. Stillness is the most damning signal an executive receives and the least attributable. A stalled programme in which the supplier has nothing left to execute alone looks identical, from above, to a stalled programme in which the supplier stopped working. The consequence Judgement forms in the gap Adverse assessments are most often formed during a stall — the exact period in which the supplier has least ability to change the picture and the record has least new data. Whatever instrument you use must therefore be able to say who the stall was waiting for. If it cannot, it will attribute the delay to whoever is easiest to invoice against. None of this argues that a supplier is usually blameless. It argues that the cheap reading is unreliable in both directions — and that a client who wants to be right, rather than merely decisive, needs three columns rather than one.
title: The Progress Record

text: PART II The record Three artefacts, all maintained jointly and all agreed in week one. No assessment in this booklet adds anything to them — that is the point of setting them up first.
title: The Progress Record

text: 2.1 One tracker, jointly maintained Named at kick-off as the tracker of record. Ideally it is yours, in your systems, under your control — a supplier-held tracker is a supplier’s account of events, however carefully kept. Six columns, and why each one is load-bearing Activity One line per discrete deliverable, small enough to be finished inside a week. An activity that cannot complete in a week hides its own delay. Workstream Groups activities so predictability can be read per stream rather than per programme. This is what reveals that variance is concentrated rather than general. Owner Us, you, or joint — and where joint, which side gates it. The single most consequential column in the file, and the one most often left to drift. Page 9 is about nothing else. Target week Set once at kick-off and not quietly revised. A target that moves with reality measures nothing. Status Not started, in progress, blocked, done. Blocked is a distinct state — collapsing it into in-progress is how wait states become invisible. Blocked by What the item is waiting for and since when. Populated at the time, by whoever notices — not reconstructed later, because reconstruction is where memory becomes advocacy. What we will not do Keep a second, private tracker that tells a better story. If our reading of progress differs from the tracker’s, the tracker is what we bring to the review and our disagreement goes in as a note beside it. What we will do Update it weekly whether or not it flatters us, and flag a blocked item the week it blocks rather than at the review. An impairment raised on the day is a fact; the same impairment raised in a dispute is an excuse, and we know the difference cuts against us. The Progress workbook keeps the same record digitally. It is available on request.
title: The Progress Record

text: 2.2 The ownership column Almost every unfair progress assessment we have seen or received comes from reading status without ownership. Four values, agreed in week one, and the third is the one that matters. Consultant-owned We can finish it without waiting for anyone. If this is late, that is ours — no denominator argument applies and we will not attempt one. Client-owned Your decision, your sign-off, your subject-matter expert, your access grant. We can chase it, escalate it and re-plan around it. We cannot complete it, and no quantity of additional effort from us moves it. Joint, client-gated The honest category Both parties have work in it, but ours cannot start until yours lands. Most trackers record these simply as “joint”, which reads at review as shared fault and in practice is not. Naming the gate in week one is what stops a structural dependency being remembered later as a mutual failure. Joint, consultant-gated The mirror case, and it exists. Your people cannot proceed until we deliver something. When these age, the finding is against us and page 17 governs what follows. The discipline this imposes on us Ownership is set at kick-off and taken verbatim from the tracker at review — we do not reclassify an item as client-owned once it is late. If we believe an owner is wrong, we raise it that week, in the tracker, where you can see it and contest it. An ownership column edited during a dispute is worth nothing to either of us. A programme can be genuinely behind while its supplier is genuinely complete. Those are not contradictory findings, and an instrument that cannot report both at once will report the wrong one.

text: The model layer under IDDC The machines calculate. People do the thinking. Every piece of this work keeps the cognitive part of the job with people: framing the question, weighing what matters, choosing, and answering for the choice. AI and automation are used hard, for speed and reach, but only ever to propose. That is the difference you are buying. Stays with people Framing. What the decision really is, and whose it is. Judgement. What counts, what is protected, what trade-off is acceptable. Deciding. The choice is made and signed by a named person with the authority. Accountability. section: What the models are not allowed to do
text: The model layer under IDDC What the models are not allowed to do The IDDC discipline binds the model layer as tightly as it binds us. Five rules travel with every calculation the model layer permits. 01 No unlabelled number Every model output carries its pedigree — estimated — and a range. text: Part Six · From the work Why every number should say where it came from A figure in a board pack carries authority whether or not it deserves it. A number someone typed in, a number from a published table and a number from a model all look the same on a slide. We label every figure with its pedigree: observed, declared, taken from a published source, or estimated. Estimates carry ranges. In our Employer Report, the audit trail marks each hiring stage as “explicit” when a recruiter recorded it and “inferred” when the system deduced it. This makes discussion faster. People stop arguing about whether a number is right and start asking how much weight it can bear. Try this. In your next management pack, add one small column to the key table: source. When the CFO and the shop steward read the same page The CFO asks what something costs. The COO asks where the time goes. Employee relations asks whether a decision will stand at the CCMA. Organised labour asks whether workers will carry the burden. All four questions are fair. Most reports answer one of them. Our diagnostics produce one result and render it for each chair. In the sample, five of six stakeholder views ranked the same structural problem first, even though a purely financial ranking would have deferred it. text: Two of three Clarity without surveillance There is a fair fear about any tool that measures how work gets done. It can become a way of watching people rather than understanding systems. In South Africa, with its history and its labour law, that fear deserves a direct answer. Our answer is built into the instruments, not left to good intentions. We measure systems, not people. In the Organisational Debt Diagnostic, every finding attaches to a system, a process, a decision or a role. Time is sampled anonymously and reported only for groups of five or more. There are no individual scores, rankings or lists of names. Proposals to add person-level fields are refused by design. We exclude the data from people decisions. Engagement terms prohibit using diagnostic data for disciplinary, incapacity, appraisal or retrenchment-selection purposes. We share governance. Where there is organised labour or a workplace forum, we recommend a joint governance body with audit rights over how the data is used. Staff receive their own plain-language view of the findings. Where an instrument does assess an individual, as a hiring report must, we apply stricter rules. Components without evidence are excluded, not treated as neutral. Background checks never trigger an automated rejection. Psychometric inputs must meet the Employment Equity Act’s requirement that tests be scientifically valid, reliable, fairly applied and not biased. Candidates can respond to the reasoning, and the decision stays with the employer. The reward for this discipline is trust, and trust is what makes measurement accurate. People answer honestly when they know the answer cannot be used against them. The findings are usually a relief: the friction was never their fault, and now there is evidence to say so.

text: ONE The light that was rationed For decades, a clear view of how an organisation actually spends its time, money and judgement was something most South African businesses could not buy. It existed. It was simply rationed.
title: Seeing Clearly

text: Part One Who could see A listed bank or insurer preparing for a restructure could commission a large advisory firm. Teams of analysts would arrive, interview dozens of people, model costs, and deliver a report. Those reports often told leadership things they had sensed but could never prove: where the rework sat, which approvals were slowing everything down, what staff turnover was really costing. That work was expensive, slow and relationship-driven. It was sold to organisations that already had the budget, the procurement channel and the partner relationships. It was usually delivered once, as a document, and then aged on a shelf. Who could not Everyone else made the same decisions with far less light. A mid-sized manufacturer set salaries from last year’s survey and instinct. A recruiter placed candidates without knowing whether the offer was economically survivable for the person accepting it. An HR team faced a CCMA referral without a record of why a decision had been made. A family business lost a key person and discovered that half the operation lived in that person’s head. These organisations were not less capable. They were less equipped. They carried the same costs, but the costs were invisible, so nobody could manage them.

Render and hand over. Views for finance, operations, technology, employee relations, organised labour, staff and the executive, all from the one file. Different weightings, identical numbers. Review. Data is returned or destroyed on schedule. The baseline, definitions and versions stay with you. On the review date the instrument is re-run, and the comparison is the point. What I need from you A named decision owner with authority. Access to the relevant extracts. Roughly six to ten hours of your people's time across the engagement. Permission to brief staff honestly about what's being measured. What you won't be asked for A data warehouse, a platform purchase or a full population census. section: What I stand behind, and what I don't
text: What I stand behind, and what I don't The right-hand column is the one that matters. A commitment without stated exclusions is a sales line that gets disclaimed in an annexure nobody read. I stand behind The arithmetic. Every figure can be re-derived from the inputs at the stamped versions. That the method was followed, item by item, and anyone can check it. That the pedigree is honest. Nothing estimated is shown as observed, and thin sources are labelled thin. That it reproduces. Same inputs and versions give the same answer, or it's a defect. That the data is handled as agreed. Minimised, reported in groups of five or more, returned or destroyed on schedule. I don't stand behind Any commercial outcome. A finding doesn't guarantee a saving. What happens next is a decision I name but don't take. Inputs I didn't measure. A figure you supply is marked declared: I warrant my use of it, not its accuracy. Individual behaviour. An estimate is a probability over a population, never evidence about a named person. Legal, tax, audit or actuarial conclusions, or compliance itself. The work supports King IV and the employment statutes; it doesn't discharge them. This is the spirit of the Decision Warranty: it warrants that the process was followed. It doesn't promise an outcome, and it isn't insurance.

text: The engineering thinking framework Four thinking skills sit under everything: decomposition, algorithms, pattern recognition and abstraction. The work then climbs an abstraction layer, descends a logical continuum into something that runs, and is kept alive by life-cycling. Three engineering domains do the building, with support and additional domains behind them. Read top to bottom. The abstraction layer is always held in context; the domains at the foot are where the building is done, with the support and additional domains serving them. Step What it does Abstraction layer Moves from problem to opportunity, options, choices and hypotheses; from concept through a schematic or visual to a logical form; and from principles through key business questions (KBQ) to purpose, goals and objectives. All of it is held in context, so that nothing is decided in the abstract. Logical continuum The logical form becomes a physical model, then a mathematical, operations research or simulation model, then a prototype that can be tried. Life-cycling Versioning management and optimisation turn the prototype into a solution that can be kept, changed and retired in good order. Domains Decision, Coherence and Meaning Engineering are the three that carry the work. Model-Driven Software Engineering, Mathematical Engineering and Site Reliability Engineering support them. Evidence and Implementation are additional domains. Pattern recognition earns its place by saving effort. CQRS, for instance, keeps the write model apart from the read models, so each can be shaped for its own job.

text: Product principles A product here is not a deliverable that happens to work. It is built from four principles, and judged against eight qualities. Product thinking Think of the thing as something that will be used again, by people, and will have to change. Design for that life, not for the handover. Inherent value Meaning by default. The default semantics are right, so the product is correct without configuration, and a user has to work to make it wrong. Designed with purpose Every part answers a stated purpose. What cannot be tied to one is removed. User-centred The user is the person who must decide, act or answer for the result, and the product is shaped around what that person needs to know. What makes a product good Useful It serves a decision or task that someone actually has. Usable The people it is for can use it without special help. Understandable Its logic and its results can be explained in plain terms. Trustworthy Honest about its limits: it says what it does not cover and how sure it is. Coherent Its parts agree with one another and with the meanings it declares. Maintainable and evolvable It can be corrected and extended without breaking what depends on it. Efficient It uses no more effort and resource than the purpose warrants. Accountable Every output can be traced to its sources, its rules and its owner. Two words set the ambition. Better means the product measurably improves the decision it serves. Beyond means it changes which decisions are possible at all.

text: Requirement categories Requirements are sorted by kind, because each kind is tested, owned and changed in a different way. Category What it states Functional What the product does: the behaviour a user can observe. Non-functional How well it does it: the quality attributes, such as accuracy, speed, availability, security and explainability. Constraining (specification) A limit on how the product may be built or run, set from outside the design: a standard, a platform, a jurisdiction, a format. Business rule A rule of the organisation that the product must apply or respect, owned by the business and not by the engineers. Architectural contract The interface and the invariant that other parts may rely on. It is promised to the rest of the system, so changing it is a breaking change.

text: Layers The medallion runs from Bronze to Silver to Gold. Two planes sit alongside it rather than above it, and promotion between layers is by contract. BronzeRaw and immutable, landed exactly as received. SilverIntegrated, source-aligned history. GoldShaped for each consumer, compiled from what lies beneath. Semantic PlatinumA plane of governed meaning: definitions, ontology and metric semantics. Abstraction DiamondA plane of decision-ready abstractions: the models and instruments that decisions are made on. The two planes are alongside, not on top, because meaning and abstraction apply at every medallion layer. They are not a fourth and fifth step that data climbs. Promotion by contract Data moves between layers only through six promotion gates, P1 to P6. Each gate is a contract check, and each check is held under one of three enforcement classes. Class Meaning E · Enforced A machine applies the check and blocks promotion if it fails. M · Monitored A machine watches and raises a flag, and a person decides what follows. A · Attested An accountable person states that it holds, and their name stays on the record. This works with a Data Mesh, where domains own their products, and with a Logical Data Fabric or virtual ODS, where data is queried in place. The planes are what keep meaning consistent across domains.

text: The tripod A product stands on three legs. A short leg is not made up for by a long one. Effectiveness The right thing: it does what the decision actually needs. Efficiency The right cost and effort: no more than the purpose warrants. Excellence The right quality and craft: it is made properly and will hold. The Tripod Floor is the rule that keeps this honest: no product ships if any one leg is below its floor, however strong the other two are.

section: Mining, as a way of discovering
text: Mining, as a way of discovering Mining runs the architecture in reverse. Instead of building from intent toward evidence, it starts from what is there and works out what is actually happening. It has seven disciplines. Discipline What it looks for Data mining Patterns and structure in the data itself. Decision mining The decisions that are really being made, and on what. Process mining The process as it runs, against the process as described. Coherence mining Where decisions, rules and measures disagree with one another. Meaning mining The meanings in use, and where one term carries several. Evidence mining What is relied on, and what it rests on. Outcome mining What followed, and how it connects to what was decided. Findings do not go straight into the design. Each enters as a Discovery Case, which is examined before anything is built on it.

text: Correction and semantic state Things said in a product will sometimes be wrong. The design makes correcting them visible, and makes meaning behave like state that is managed. The correction plane A claim can be revised or withdrawn, and the trail stays visible and versioned. Nothing is silently overwritten. I think of it as an “unsay” pattern: to unsay something, you say so, on the record. Semantic state Every term and every claim has a type and a lifecycle. Only legal transitions are allowed, so a term cannot move from draft to retired without passing through the states between. The constitutional layer The axioms the product rests on are held in their own layer and declared, not scattered through the rules. Changing one is a constitutional change, handled as such.

text: Epistemic typing This is the newest part of the doctrine, and I hold it more tentatively than the rest. It asks a plain question of every claim a product makes: what kind of claim is this, and so what could count against it? Three things that can look alike Kind What it is Verdict Meaningless No defined subject, domain or interpretation. It is not even false. Cannot be tested, and cannot be relied on. Unfalsifiable by kind Values, axioms and constitutive commitments. They are not the sort of thing evidence settles. Legitimate, if declared as what they are. Immunised Testable in principle, but worded or governed so that nothing may count against it. This can happen by wording, by compression or by capture. The pathology. The rule: absence of falsification is not truth, and prevention of falsification is evidence against the claim. Every claim is typed In a product, each claim is given one of eight types: value, belief about reality, empirical hypothesis, assumption, preference, causal claim, warrant or authority. The type decides what evidence is owed. Creed is not fact, and neither is warrant: a creed is declared, a fact is observed, and a warrant is the ground on which reliance is placed. Four forms of institutional belief Form Where it shows Declared What the institution says it believes. Embedded What its rules and metrics assume. Revealed What its repeated, costly choices show. Presupposed What must be true for its reasoning to make sense at all. Gaps between the four are measurable incoherence. Argyris and Schön called the first gap espoused theory against theory-in-use; organisational studies call a related one decoupling. How a creed defends itself A creed is not proved. It is declared, and kept contestable. Whether it is healthy shows in how it defends itself, in the sense Lakatos gave to research programmes. Progressive It absorbs contrary evidence by making new commitments, and those commitments turn out to be right. Degenerating It meets contrary evidence with ad hoc reinterpretation, each one protecting the creed and adding nothing. Single and double loop Single-loop learning corrects actions. Double-loop learning can revise the creed itself, and it needs a protected, independent and authorised challenge process. Preference laundering A preference is built into rules or metrics, and the result is then presented as what “the process produced”. The counter is to require every material outcome to trace to a named decision record, so that a person, not a process, is visibly the one who chose. The principleInstitutional belief may govern action; it may not govern whether the belief itself is contestable. The framework applies this to itself. It declares its own axioms and its own revision path, and it is open to the same challenge it asks of others.

text: The Disciplined Decision Cycle IDDC, the Ingqiqo Disciplined Decision Cycle, turns evidence and business meaning into decisions that can be checked, contested and repeated. It begins from an established data-modelling discipline and extends past it into execution and outcome learning. Discover. Find the decision, the people who hold it, and the evidence that exists. Connect. Tie the evidence to shared meaning: terms, entities and relationships. Review. Test the evidence and the assumptions against a clear standard. Facilitate. Bring the decision-holders together on the same picture. Compare. Lay out the alternatives, and what each one gives up. Consolidate. Settle on one decision, recorded with its evidence and authority. Publish. Release it as a governed record that others can rely on and contest. Execute. Carry it out within declared bounds, watching for deviation. Learn. Score the outcome separately from the process, and feed the difference back. The cycle sits where business architecture, knowledge engineering, decision intelligence, operations research and AI governance meet. Its constitution sets out roles, evidence standards, an epistemic ladder, decision contracts, solver policies, contestation and outcome learning, and it grows by addition rather than by removing what came before.

text: How decisions are understood Not every decision is a calculation. The method distinguishes how a decision is produced before it judges whether it was good. Rational Deliberate weighing of options against stated objectives and constraints: the territory of optimisation and the solver. Behavioural Choices shaped by framing, reference points and bias. The method debiases openly; it never nudges a principal toward its own recommendation. Nature-driven Outcomes produced by thresholds, selection and emergence rather than by anyone choosing. These are named as such, so nobody is blamed for a decision nobody made. A second axis runs across all three: ordinary, tradeable values versus protected values. Protected values are treated as hard limits on what may be chosen, never as heavy weights that a large enough gain could buy out.

text: A short glossary The words the method relies on, in plain terms. Pedigree Where a figure came from, and how far it can be trusted: observed, declared, published or estimated. Stakeholder view A version of one canonical result written for a specific role, such as the CFO, the COO or organised labour. Different weightings, never different numbers. Decision record A dated account of what was decided, on what information, by whose authority, with a review date. Decision Canvas A twelve-field record for a significant decision, with eight-, five- and three-field variants for lower stakes. Decision Governance Standard Seventeen principles for governing decisions, in four pillars: integrity, accountability, coherence and learning. Organisational debt Any unfinished rule, definition, system or decision that makes today's work slower or riskier. Carrying cost The annual cost of work done to compensate for unfinished past decisions, above a normal coordination allowance. Coordination floor The share of time treated as the normal cost of working together, and excluded from carrying cost. Truck factor How many people could leave before a critical rule set can no longer be applied. Cost of acceptance The employer's full first-year cost of a hire: recruitment, onboarding, ramp-up and total cost to company. Decision IR The single typed record every decision compiles into: intent, evidence, assumptions, objectives, constraints and authority. Decision Warranty A warranty that the process was followed and the record is true. It doesn't promise an outcome, and it isn't insurance.
title: The Method

section: Human in the loop, by design
text: Human in the loop, by design The method uses AI and automation hard, for speed and reach, and never lets them do the thinking. The cognitive work of deciding stays with people at every step of the cycle. Step The person The machine Discover · Connect Names the decision and who owns it Finds and links the evidence, with its source Review · Compare Judges what counts and what is protected Calculates options, ranges and trade-offs Facilitate · Consolidate Weighs, chooses and signs Proposes, explains and records each proposal Publish · Execute Holds the authority and answers for it Watches for deviation within declared bounds Learn Decides what the outcome teaches Scores process and outcome separately No model sets a weight, asserts a constraint or issues a decision. That is the promise to a client: the speed of AI, with judgement and accountability kept where a board, a regulator or a court will look for them.

title: From the work

text: Nkosinathi Mbambo From the work The cost no one counts Short pieces for managers, HR practitioners, owners and boards. Each ends with something you can try this week. Every organisation already spends heavily on its decisions: on hiring, on meetings, on rework, on waiting. Very few can see that spending clearly. These notes show what it looks like once it's measured.
title: From the work

text: Short pieces The examples come from illustrative samples built on fictitious organisations. They aren't client data, and they aren't a prediction for any particular organisation. Hiring What does it really cost to say yes to a job offer? Most offers are judged from one side. The employer asks whether the package fits the budget. Almost nobody asks whether it fits the life of the person accepting it. In an illustrative Employer Report, a senior offer that looked affordable left the candidate almost nothing each month after housing, commute, school fees and debt. A modest rise in their living costs flipped the recommendation to reject, and the estimated chance of the hire leaving within a year was 38 per cent. None of this means “don't hire”. It means hire with open eyes: adjust the package, the start date or the relocation support, or accept the risk knowingly and record why. Try thisFor your next senior offer, list the candidate's likely fixed costs next to the net salary. If the gap is under ten per cent, have that conversation before signing. Time The one-day-in-five problem Ask a team where its time goes and you'll hear “meetings” and “email”. Measure it properly and a different picture appears. In an illustrative diagnostic of a 180-person claims department, about 22 per cent of working time went on four things: searching for answers nobody wrote down, redoing work after definition disputes, waiting for approvals, and meetings that read a dashboard aloud. Eight per cent was allowed as the normal cost of working together; the rest was drain. The important finding wasn't the size. It was the cause. Almost none of it came from lack of effort. It came from things left unfinished upstream. Try thisFor one week, ask your team to note each time they wait, search or redo. Group the notes by cause, not by person. Knowledge Your most important rule may live in two people's heads Every organisation has a rule set that “just works”: how exceptions are approved, how a special case is priced. Often it works because one or two long-serving people carry it. I measure this as a truck factor: how many people would need to leave before the rule can no longer be applied. In the sample, the exception rules had a truck factor of one, only five per cent of answers came from documentation, and new staff took seven months to reach full speed. It's always reported for the asset, never for the people who hold it. One team's response: “Finally, someone's going to write this down so we can take leave.” Try thisList your five most critical rule sets. For each, count who could apply it tomorrow without asking anyone. Decisions An open decision is not a free decision Leaders sometimes delay a hard call to keep options open. The delay feels costless. It rarely is. In the sample, a decision about outsourcing one function had been open for fourteen months. Two teams were staffing for both possible futures, the affected staff lived with uncertainty, and any later consultation would start from low trust. The answer isn't always to decide immediately. Sometimes the right move is a small, funded option: a sixty-day design exercise with a clear review date and a trigger for reopening. Try thisList every significant decision older than ninety days. Give each an owner, a date, and either a decision or a defined option. Evidence Why every number should say where it came from A figure in a board pack carries authority whether or not it deserves it. A number someone typed in, a number from a published table and a number from a model all look the same on a slide. Every figure I produce carries its pedigree: observed, declared, taken from a published source, or estimated. Estimates carry ranges. Even an audit trail marks each step as explicit, when someone recorded it, or inferred, when a system deduced it. People stop arguing about whether a number is right and start asking how much weight it can bear. Try thisIn your next management pack, add one small column to the key table: source. Stakeholders When the CFO and the shop steward read the same page The CFO asks what something costs. The COO asks where the time goes. Employee relations asks whether a decision will stand at the CCMA. Organised labour asks whether workers will carry the burden. All four questions are fair. One result, rendered for each chair, changes the conversation. In the sample, five of six stakeholder views ranked the same structural problem first, even though a purely financial ranking would have deferred it. When everyone works from the same number, disagreement becomes about priorities, which can be discussed, rather than facts, which shouldn't need to be. Try thisBefore your next contested decision, ask each stakeholder to rank cost, risk, people and long-term structure privately. Compare the rankings before the meeting. Accountability A good outcome is not a good decision When something goes wrong, the search for who is to blame often starts before anyone has established what was knowable at the time. Choosing the forum that judges an event can quietly choose the verdict. Five tests catch manufactured culpability: who chose the forum; whether the evidence standard was applied equally to everyone; when each piece of information became available; where it came from; and whether the question is being judged in the right domain at all. Recording the frame before a decision, and what was knowable at the moment it was made, is what lets accountability land where it belongs rather than where it's easiest. Try thisFor your next significant decision, write down three things before you choose: the frame, what you know now, and what you don't. Human in the loop The machines calculate. People do the thinking. A general-purpose language model produces the most plausible next word. That's a reasonable way to draft a paragraph and an unsound way to price a hire, size a pay gap or estimate a year of rework. A board can't audit a sentence that merely sounded right. So the line is drawn hard. Machines calculate, retrieve, propose and record. People frame the question, weigh what matters, decide and answer for it. No model sets a weight, asserts a constraint or issues a decision, and every machine contribution is logged as a proposal someone accepted or rejected. Try thisFor one AI-assisted output you rely on, ask who accepted it, on what basis, and where that acceptance is written down.
title: From the work

text: At length Three longer arguments for executives, boards and governance committees. One of three Decisions are assets: govern them like capital Boards govern capital with care. Every rand is budgeted, approved, recorded, audited and reviewed. Decisions receive almost none of that discipline, even though capital moves only because someone decided it should. Ask most organisations three questions about a decision made last year and the answers fall away. What was known at the time? What alternatives were considered? Who had the authority, and when was it to be reviewed? The Decision Governance Standard sets four conditions: integrity (sufficient, verified, traceable information), accountability (a named decision-maker, rationale, authority and review date), coherence (decisions don't quietly contradict each other) and learning (outcomes compared with intentions). The Decision Canvas scales with the stakes: a board resolution uses all twelve fields; a routine rule-governed decision records three. Two of three Clarity without surveillance There's a fair fear about any tool that measures how work gets done: it can become a way of watching people rather than understanding systems. In South Africa, with its history and its labour law, that fear deserves a direct answer. The answer is built into the instruments. Findings attach to systems, processes, decisions and roles. Time is sampled anonymously and reported only for groups of five or more. Diagnostic data is contractually barred from disciplinary, appraisal or retrenchment-selection use. Where labour is organised, a joint governance body holds audit rights. The reward is trust, and trust is what makes measurement accurate. The findings are usually a relief: the friction was never people's fault, and now there's evidence to say so. Three of three Access is the point South Africa's economy runs on organisations that have never had a strategy team: mid-sized manufacturers, family businesses, municipal entities, independent recruiters, schools, clinics and co-operatives. Most make their consequential decisions with the least support. Three shifts change that. The method can be written down, so quality no longer depends on a large team. The instrument can be reused, so the second run costs a fraction of the first. And the standards can be open, using formats like DMN decision tables and YAML contracts, so nobody is locked into a black box. A sixty-person business should see where its time goes, whether its offers are sound and whether its decisions can be defended, with the rigour a listed bank expects.

text: What it gives you If you want to choose a change-data-capture tool on evidence rather than habit, A reproducible head-to-head on your own source, with a decision recorded per leg of the architecture and every figure traceable to a run.
title: CDC head-to-head: Debezium, Airbyte, OLake

text: The problem Change data capture is where the lakebase's truth becomes everyone else's events. Tools are usually chosen on a vendor page or a colleague's habit, and the choice then shapes the broker, the lakehouse and the cost of every replay for years.
title: CDC head-to-head: Debezium, Airbyte, OLake

text: Approach Point all three tools at the same Postgres lakebase, with logical replication on and synthetic data only. Seed the same rows, then apply the same seeded workload of inserts, updates and deletes, each change carrying a unique sequence number so arrival can be checked exactly. Measure snapshot time, change-to-arrival latency (p50 and p95), burst throughput, ordering per key, delete and tombstone handling, a column added mid-run, kill-and-restart recovery (duplicates and gaps) and resource footprint. Write every number to a results file from the harness only; a value nobody measured prints as "not yet measured", never as an estimate. Decide per leg, not overall: the event leg and the lakehouse leg ask different things of change capture.
title: CDC head-to-head: Debezium, Airbyte, OLake

text: Design fit, from the documentation What each tool is built to do, read from its own documentation. This is not a measurement, and it is where the measurement will either agree or embarrass it. Debezium Log-based streaming of row changes into Kafka, which is the shape the event leg already has. A delete arrives as a delete plus a tombstone. Delivery is exactly-once in normal running and at-least-once after a crash, which is why the projector deduplicates by event id. Costs: row changes rather than decision events. The reference stack now runs it as Debezium Server, a single process that writes into NATS JetStream with no Kafka Connect cluster to operate; the Kafka Connect form remains for the comparison. OLake Built for Postgres to Apache Iceberg, with full refresh plus change capture through pgoutput and an upsert mode that deduplicates. It fits the analytical leg, history in the lakehouse, rather than the event bus: it runs as sync-and-exit batches, so its latency is a batch property. Airbyte An ELT platform with a UI, the broadest connector catalogue and scheduled syncs. It is the heaviest to run, and its Kafka destination appends without deduplicating, so the consumer must dedupe (the projector already does). It needs care with replication-slot retention, or a sync fails until the slot is recreated.
title: CDC head-to-head: Debezium, Airbyte, OLake

text: Position, provisional Decided per leg, pending the run. Debezium for the event leg, where order, deletes and replay matter most. OLake for the lakehouse leg, where volume into Iceberg matters more than milliseconds. Airbyte where the source is one of the many systems the other two don't reach. text: What it gives you If you want to know whether the evidence, and the AI, behind a decision can bear its weight, Every claim rated, every estimate replayable, and every AI contribution recorded as a proposal a person accepted or rejected.
title: Decision Evidence Lab

text: The problem Many decisions cite evidence that does not bear the weight placed on it, and AI estimates now arrive with a confidence they have not earned. The gap is rarely dishonesty; it is untested inference.
title: Decision Evidence Lab

text: Approach State each decision as a claim with the evidence offered for it, and rate that evidence on a ladder from anecdote to tested causal finding. Use tabular in-context-learning models (TabDPT-Turbo and TabICLv2) for fast, distributional estimates on modest data, while pinning context rows, order and decoding so every estimate replays. Hold the causal boundary: these models are correlational, so an estimate may never be bound to a decision variable without causal support. Run open-source models such as Laya inside the client boundary as proposers only, and record their influence on the decision explicitly. Score process quality at decision time and outcome quality after; good process with a bad outcome updates the forecast, bad process with a good outcome raises a flag.

text: What it gives you If you want decisions that can be checked, repeated and warranted, not just documented, Decisions compiled into one typed record, solved within declared limits, kept on a tamper-evident ledger, and backed by a warranty of process.
title: Decision IR and the Warranty

text: The problem Decisions are the most consequential artefacts an organisation produces, and the least recorded. Months later, nobody can show what was decided, on what evidence, by whom, or what was given up to get there.
title: Decision IR and the Warranty

text: Approach Compile strategy, ontology terms, mastered identities, business rules and evidence into one typed, content-addressed Decision IR. Nothing bypasses it. Gate with GoRules, then solve on the Sovereign Logic Engine: weighted MaxSMT on Z3 over DPLL(T) and CDCL. The relaxation set, what was given up, returns with every answer. Write each decision to a hash-chained ledger: SHA3-256 links, ML-DSA signatures per entry, SLH-DSA checkpoints, with every entry recording its algorithms for crypto-agility. Trace outcomes back through the Motive, Ownership and Institutional Architecture models; the nine-step IDDC, run from discover to learn, shows where culpability was manufactured by design and who the original mover was. Warrant process fidelity, not outcomes: the decision was made as specified, on the evidence recorded, by the authority named.
